html:
Srinivasa Ramanujan was a mathematician from Tamil Nadu, born in 1887, who taught himself much of what he knew and produced thousands of results that mathematicians are still working through.

He grew up in Kumbakonam in a poor Brahmin family. A book of formulas, read in his teens, set him off. He failed college exams because he neglected every subject but maths, and worked as a clerk at the Madras port while filling notebooks with results.

In 1913 he wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, sending pages of theorems. Hardy saw at once that they were the work of a genius and brought him to Trinity College in 1914. Together they found a formula for counting the ways to split a number into sums. In 1918 he was elected to the Royal Society.

His work covered infinite series, continued fractions, numbers and mock theta functions, in the Indian tradition of series work. He was often ill in England and returned home in 1919. He died in 1920, aged 32. A "lost notebook" found in 1976 still feeds research today.
